In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I pray for blessing and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and whoever is guided by his guidance and takes his sunnah as his way until the Day of Judgement. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings.

To proceed: the man of reason who realises that he is in a confrontation and a war must prepare the provision for that confrontation, and must distinguish between his enemy and his friend. In this abode God has decreed open fronts for us, and among the most dangerous and most galling and most severe of these fronts is the front of Iblis, because of the number of his soldiers and their variety — for he has soldiers among mankind and soldiers among the jinn.

He swore by the might of God that he would lead astray most of humankind, and his oath has been realised in most of them, as God informed of that: {He said: By Your might, I shall surely lead them all astray, except Your servants among them who are sincere} (Sūrat Ṣād 38:82–83). And God, exalted be He, said: {And Iblis proved true his opinion of them, and they followed him, except a party of the believers} (Sūrat Sabaʾ 34:20). So his oath came true in leading astray most of humankind. For this reason God, exalted be He, said: {but most people do not believe} (Sūrat Hūd 11:17). And He said: {And if you obey most of those in the earth, they will lead you astray from the path of God} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:116).

So most of creatures are of the soldiers of Iblis, and this shows us that great numbers are not a necessary accompaniment of victory. Rather God, exalted be He, said: {How many a small band has overcome a large band by God's leave} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:249).

There is no doubt that God has decreed prospering and triumph for His party, those who affirm His oneness, and has decreed loss and ruin for the party of Satan, the losers. He, exalted be He, said: {Truly the party of God — they are the ones who prosper} (Sūrat al-Mujādalah 58:22). And He said: {Truly the party of God — they are the victors} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:56). And He said: {Truly the party of Satan — they are the losers} (Sūrat al-Mujādalah 58:19).

Taking Satan as an enemy requires of you that you diminish his soldiers; and the diminishing of his soldiers cannot be realised except by willing that and striving for it. This is what God accepts, and this is what a person is rewarded for.

The real victory over Satan is not by killing the greatest possible number of his followers and his soldiers, but rather by returning them to their right mind and placing them in the other party, the party of God. Transferring individuals from being of the party of Satan and his soldiers to becoming of the party of God and of those who strive in the path of God is the greatest victory over Iblis. For this reason the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said to Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, when he gave him the banner on the day of Khaybar: "For God to guide a single man by you is better for you than red camels."

The diminishing of the soldiers of Iblis is the reality of enmity towards him, and it is that by which you are able to harm him — because you are not able to kill him, since God has guaranteed him survival for the duration of this world: {Truly you are among those granted respite, until the day of the appointed time} (Sūrat al-Ḥijr 15:37–38). Nor is he harmed by the foul speech directed at him, for God has already cursed him. So with what do you harm Iblis? You harm him, and realise your enmity towards him, only by diminishing his helpers; and the most effective form of that is to bring them into the party of God and to make them among those who help God.

For this reason the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, when the angel of the mountains offered him to bring the two mountains crashing together upon the people of Mecca, said: "No — for I hope that God will bring forth from their loins men who will worship God, associating nothing with Him."

So the victory of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, over Iblis is Khalid ibn al-Walid standing in the ranks facing the party of Satan, striving in the path of God; and Abu Sufyan ibn Harb standing beneath the banner of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, striving in the path of God, having lost his right eye on the day of al-Taif beneath the banner of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and lost his left eye on the day of Yarmuk beneath the banner of his son Yazid — all of that in the path of God.

Among the manifestations of this victory also is Safwan ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf standing and fighting in the path of God and raiding the Byzantines in their own lands, raising the banner of the oneness of God (tawḥīd). And among its manifestations is the going forth of Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl — Amr ibn Hisham — raising his sword in the face of the enemies whom God summoned the bedouin to fight, namely the Banu Hanifah at al-Yamamah. For God sent down upon His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace: {Say to those of the bedouin who stayed behind: You will be called against a people of great might; you will fight them or they will submit. So if you obey, God will give you a goodly reward; and if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment} (Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:16). So Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl was one of the commanders of Islam who fought those people and who acquitted themselves well.

And among the manifestations of the victory of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, over Iblis is that the sons of those who associated partners with God, who were raised upon that association in the laps of their fathers and mothers, were the ones who broke the idols — like the sons of Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who used to smear his idol with filth, and tied it together with a dead dog and threw it into a well; and that was the cause of the acceptance of Islam by Amr ibn al-Jamuh.

Victory over Iblis is possible in every age. It is that a person should set his purpose upon one of the most obdurate enemies of God and one of the friends of Iblis, and strive for his guidance and strive to set him up in the believing rank that strives in the path of God and raises the banner of Islam. If that is realised for him, he has been able to gain a victory over Iblis and to achieve a victory in this long-drawn-out war with this bitter enemy.

Iblis has many stratagems, among the greatest of which is that he does not despair of a person except at the death-throes. So he does not cease to covet turning a person away from the path of God for the whole duration of his life.

He attempts with him the falling into associating partners with God (shirk), whether intending it deliberately, or heedless, or ignorant — he casts him into associating partners with God. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, used to seek refuge in God from that, saying: "O God, I seek refuge in You from associating anything with You while I know, and I ask Your forgiveness for what I do not know."

Then if he despairs of bringing him into associating partners with God, he attempts to cast him into one of the ruinous acts and the grave sins and the indecencies.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to turn him away from performing one of the obligatory duties of God (farāʾiḍ) and one of the pillars of Islam.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to cast him into slight lapses, into the small sins, in the hope that they may lead him to the grave ones.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to make him abandon some of the sunnah acts that complete the obligatory duties, in the hope that deficiency may enter the obligatory duties.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to cast him into the disliked acts (makrūhāt), which drag him down to the forbidden acts (muḥarramāt) if he lets himself go on in them.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to make him abandon some of the recommended acts (mandūbāt), which are a fence before the sunnah acts, and the sunnah acts are a fence before the obligatory duties.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to cast him into what is contrary to what is preferable (khilāf al-awlā), so that he may lose some of his time and waste some of his lifespan.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to occupy him with the recommended at the expense of the obligatory (wājib), and with the less excellent at the expense of the more excellent.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to cast him into excess in the obligatory duties, so that he adds to them beyond the required limit.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts with him excess also in hating the forbidden acts and in keeping away from them, until he abandons some of what is lawful for him and so forbids what God has made lawful, and thereby falls into deficiency from another direction.

These successive attempts are a net among the nets of Iblis, with which he tries to hunt the servants of God, and with which he brings down many victims every day; and they are more galling and more severe than the fall of missiles and aircraft and tanks.

Then Iblis has two standing armies: one of them is the army of appetites, and the second is the army of obscurities.

As for the army of appetites, it divides into two parts: into the sensory appetites, such as the appetite of the belly and of the private parts; and into the non-material appetites, such as the love of leadership and the love of prevailing and the craving to criticise others and to talk about them. This army — the army of appetites — few escape falling into in the whole of their lives, for a person is often in an hour of weakness and Satan entices him towards one of the appetites.

If he is able to cast him into the sensory appetites, as is the condition of many of those who have fallen into the snares of Iblis and his deception, he responds to that. But if his soul rises above that and this world has no influence upon him, he attempts to cast him down by the non-material appetites.

If he is unable to do that, he attempts to make attractive to him a kind of appetite of another sort, namely the love of discovering what others conceal from him, or the love of criticising them so that he sets himself up as a judge over them; or he may attempt, within these appetites, to make worship itself an appetite for him, so that he practises it by way of appetite and not by way of devotion. So he goes to the prayer purified and having performed the ablution, but does not do that seeking God's good pleasure; rather he does it as a habit and an appetite that he has fallen into and grown accustomed to from the time of his fathers and grandfathers.

As for the second army, the army of obscurities, it likewise divides into two parts: into obscurities in dealing with God, and obscurities in dealing with people.

Then the obscurities in dealing with God divide into two parts: into obscurities of creed and obscurities of worship.

As for the obscurities of creed, he does not cease to cast upon a person kinds of obscurities, until he says to him: "This world — God created it; so who created God?" — as the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, informed of that. And he does not cease to make him doubt the matter in which there is no doubt and which none doubts but one who has disabled his reason and his innate disposition (fiṭrah) and departed from the religion of God entirely.

A person is astonished when he hears the speech of some of those who have fallen into the traps and snares of Iblis in the obscurities of creed: how they have clung to what is weaker than the weaving of a spider; and how they have left behind them the clear Book of God and the sound, explicit sunnah, and have clung to fabricated reports and weak ones and to the battered and the gored and what the wild beast has eaten, while they leave behind them the plain, open revelation which is like the sun at midday.

This is among the strange things — but whoever knows the method by which Iblis leads people astray knows that such a kind of deception is not to be thought strange of him. For we see some of the helpers of Iblis among mankind deceiving people with kinds of speech that are of the genus of sorcery, as the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, made clear: "Truly some eloquence is sorcery" — and by that they cast them into dangers and errors. So how should Iblis, who is the commander of this party and who inspired the kinds of obscurity, not be capable of this sort of confusing of people and of casting a false appearance over them?

What is astonishing is that some of those upon whom the false appearance is cast, so that they cling to what is frailer than the weaving of a spider, often do not concern themselves with studying what is beneficial and do not study sound knowledge. Rather they search out ambiguous passages of the Book, or ambiguous matters of the sunnah, or weak reports that do not rise to the degree of being used as proof, and cling to them and leave behind them the plain, clear truth in which there is no confusion and no obscurity.

Among the strangest of strange things is what some of the reformers in this age relate: that he met a man of those who cling to this kind of pretext, and the man asked him about a ruling of the revealed law, and he set out for him that ruling with its proof from the Book and with a number of prophetic reports indicating it; and the man said: "But there has come, in a report stopping at a Companion, which al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim transmitted without a chain in the Nawādir al-Uṣūl, such and such." So he said: "Is it with this that you oppose the speech of God and the sunnah of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace?"

This is of the work of Iblis. It is what makes many people gather flimsy arguments and battered and gored proofs for a matter that has no connection with them and that they have no need of, and that the whole religion has no need of. He clung to it only because Iblis tied his head to it and knotted the knots upon him, so that he is unable to escape from the net of Iblis which he knotted upon his head in any way whatever.

Likewise, among the kinds of creedal obscurity which Iblis casts is what relates to the hobby of pronouncing others unbelievers or misguided, or to excess in the texts of the revealed law on the opposite side. For we have mentioned that Iblis does not despair and does not give up except at death. So if he finds a person sound in creed in himself, and despairs of casting him into these creedal obscurities, he attempts to cast him into another kind of creedal obscurity, namely that he should pass judgement upon others with excess and depart from the beaten path. So instead of being a student of knowledge, or even a scholar or a caller to God, he passes over into being a judge who tries others without summoning them and without examining the evidence and the claims, and issues verdicts without being qualified for that.

This without doubt is of the scheming of Iblis, and it is a cause of division and dispute among humankind; and this is among the most important of what Iblis strives for. For it is established as sound (ṣaḥīḥ) from the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, that Iblis has a throne upon the water, and he sends out his raiding parties by night. One of them comes to him and says: "I did not cease with him until he committed fornication." And he says: "You have done nothing; perhaps he will repent and God will turn to him in forgiveness." Then another comes and says: "I did not cease with him until he killed." And he says: "You have done nothing; perhaps he will repent and God will turn to him in forgiveness." Then another comes and says: "I did not cease with him until he drank wine." And he says: "You have done nothing; perhaps he will repent and God will turn to him in forgiveness." Then another comes and says: "I did not cease with him until I separated between him and his wife." And he draws him near and kisses him and says: "You are my son."

He strives to divide between people in every way, and strives to bring about enmity and hatred between them. This is his striving, and he takes up for it various means, such as drinking wine, and usurious transactions, and the kinds of gambling and games of chance — all of that is among the means of bringing about hatred and rancour between people.

Some of the later people of knowledge have mentioned that politics among the later generations, and especially in the Arab world, is like wine and gambling: Satan wishes by it to cast enmity and hatred between people. For that reason you witness in our country that many ties of kinship have been severed because of political disagreements and party affiliations — and sometimes within a single party, a single family competes and there occurs between its members such hatred and rancour and severing of kinship as God knows.

God, exalted be He, said: {Truly wine and gambling and idolatrous altars and divining arrows are an abomination of Satan's work, so shun it, that you may prosper. Satan only wishes to cast enmity and hatred between you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of God and from the prayer. Will you not then desist?} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:90–91).

This prayer is what gathers hearts and joins them upon the truth; and the remembrance of God is what removes enmity and hatred: {Truly it is by the remembrance of God that hearts find rest} (Sūrat al-Raʿd 13:28) — because it is what Iblis flees from.

These many creedal obscurities spread when people are distracted from striving in the path of God and from raiding the enemy. For when the Muslims retreat and turn in upon their internal disagreements among themselves, the misleading innovations spread among them. These innovations and creedal obscurities did not become widespread in the times of striving and martyrdom and victory: when the armies of the Muslims set out raiding to the easts of the earth and its wests, you hear no word from the people of caprice and of sects, and you see no utterance of theirs. But when the armies return and people settle into ease and are occupied with the affairs of this world, the one who raises discord rises up and its caller proclaims aloud, raising his voice and raising his banner; and there gather about him those whom God has led astray.

This has been tested in the whole history of Islam. The Companions, God's good pleasure be upon them, feared when they saw many people to whom this world had opened its doors, so that they came forward to gather its fruit and did not go out on the winter campaign nor on the summer campaign; and they saw that the sitting of these people was a likely occasion for their becoming occupied with creedal obscurities. And that is what happened: the Qadariyyah sect arose, then the Jabriyyah sect, and before that the Khawarij sect, and after them the Shia sect, and so on.

As for the second kind of his obscurities in dealing with God, it is the obscurities of worship. What we see of insinuating doubts among people concerning ritual purity and the prayer and other kinds of acts of worship is all from his strenuous striving. For he strives to lessen the standing of worship in a person's eyes, so that it is of no consequence in his conception of things. Among the marks of that is its difficulty for a person and his laziness in it.

So if you see a person finding an ordinary prayer long and burdensome, and the prayer passes from its beginning to its end without his being present in a single one of its essential elements (rukn); and you see him, when the imam lengthens the recitation or lengthens the bowing or the prostration, becoming irritated and complaining — while he remains hour after hour in his shop, and may even remain an hour waiting for a taxi in the street — then know that Satan has taken hold of his reins in these obscurities of worship.

In the obscurities of worship he has built two great walls: one of them is the wall of excess and the second is the wall of negligence. And he has placed in these two walls doors, through each one of which enters whoever responds to him.

So he attempts with a person that he be negligent first, falling short in worship. For that reason you find the mosques filling up at the times of the festivals and the Friday prayers, and you find that no more than a row or two pray in them at the dawn prayer. That is only because Satan knots upon the back of people's heads three knots, striking at each knot: "You have a long night ahead of you, so sleep."

Likewise in the field of competing in the other acts of obedience: we used formerly to witness competition over the circles of the scholars and sitting with them, and competition in memorising the Book of God — and that has begun to decrease as people have increased. There is no scarcity of people, but those who desire good have begun to decrease. And that is only by his leading astray through the kinds of preoccupation he brings about, and by his alarms and his cries which he sends out through the televisions and the satellite channels and the other media; for these occupy people away from beneficial knowledge, and occupy them away from what benefits them in the affairs of their religion and their world.

Look at the sons of the noble families, whose fathers, when they reached the age these are at, would go to the study-centres and study under the shaykhs and would not return to their families until they had secured beneficial knowledge — and they were the ones to whom people turned for the preparing of funerals, or for leading the prayer, or for contracting a marriage. And today no one lifts his head to them with any of the important affairs of religion.

This is a widespread reality; and whoever disdains it or supposes it to be an attack upon him, let him review himself and his own course, and let him compare between his condition and the condition of his fathers before him.

Likewise among the kinds of obscurity of worship which he casts is what relates to the other wall, the wall of excess. He strives with some people to occupy them with the affairs of the hereafter at the expense of the affairs of this world, or with some of the affairs of the hereafter at the expense of others. So a person enters the sacred state of the prayer, and he has an address directed to him from the Lord of might at every standing and bowing and at every lowering and raising — and he occupies him with some matter of the hereafter, or with recalling one of its states, or with recalling one of his other obligatory duties, so that he is occupied by that from performing the prayer. So he has neither set right that obligatory duty and given it precedence over the prayer, nor set right the prayer, because of his being occupied away from it.

This kind of excess is likewise widespread among the committed among people. I know people who were people of misguidance and error, and God guided them to Islam — but they entered it from a narrow angle, and wanted to restrict what is broad and to narrow this revealed law in which God has made things broad for His servants. They occupied themselves with the small matters at the expense of the great ones, and lived with illusions, and by that they are in a striving that is out of place and a war upon those who are not its proper object. They have occupied themselves with slight particulars, which are like the mote at the corner of the eye, and have left calamities and great problems, being occupied away from them by what is lesser than them. So they have made of a seed a dome, and of a slight matter a great calamity.

That kind of excess is what afflicted the Christians when they innovated a monasticism which God did not permit and did not command them with; so their men of religion secluded themselves in the cells and cut themselves off from the world and denied themselves its pleasures and appetites. When Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, went out to Syria, he saw the monks in the monasteries and saw their devotion to worship and their self-expending in it and their weeping — and he wept a severe weeping. It was said to him: "Commander of the Faithful, what makes you weep?" He said: "What makes me weep is the condition of these. They are the ones of whom God said" — in the closing verses of Sūrat al-Kahf — "{Say: Shall I inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose striving went astray in the life of this world while they supposed that they were doing well in workmanship} (Sūrat al-Kahf 18:103–104)."

Those suppose that they are doing well in workmanship, and they are the ones who have strayed from the right way; and what they did avails them nothing, and all their deeds will be scattered dust on the Day of Resurrection.

That kind of excess still exists. For this reason we find that those of the Christians who accept Islam today enter Islam searching in it for monasticism, and so they often attach themselves to some of the misleading innovations, or take shelter with the people of innovation, because they see in what these have a resemblance to what they had understood religion to be in the days of their ignorance and their associating partners with God. So they often take shelter in the cells of the people of innovation and often join them, because they understood religion through that angle; and when they entered this Islam they sought in it what resembled religion in their conception of it from when they were Christians, and found nothing but those innovations, so they joined them and attached themselves to them.

As for the second kind of the obscurities, it is the obscurities in dealing with people; and these likewise divide into two parts.

The first part concerns the appraisal of people. For many people measure others only through the eye of a needle, and look at them only with a look of superiority and disdain. In their view the people of faith are not in a fortified stronghold, and the people of obedience and worship are not beyond criticism and attack in that regard.

This kind of people — you find them paying no heed to prayer nor to fasting nor to calling to God nor to striving; but whenever they see someone turning towards God in any matter whatever, they begin to revile him and abuse him and attack his intention, and say: "He did this only for show and to be heard of," and "He did such-and-such only as an innovation." They suppose that everything of the religion which they did not know is a new invention or an imported religion. Those misguided ones have known nothing of the religion but its name, and have known nothing of the sunnah but its trace, and have never travelled any of the roads of guidance. Rather they are nothing but like flies, which alight only upon filth: they seek out the errors and leave the lush meadows. They are occupied with seeking out the stumbles and slips of others.

Such people would do well to know their own worth and to review their condition, and to remember that over them are noble scribes, guardians who neither neglect nor let anything be lost; and that others likewise have those who write their deeds — so there is no need for those people to correct them and fault them, nor to attack and criticise them.

This kind of attack upon people in appraising them is the cause of the attack of the Khawarij upon the Companions of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace. For a group of the young men of Banu Asad ibn Khuzaymah at Kufa claimed that Sad ibn Abi Waqqas did not perform the prayer well, and complained of him to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him. So he asked him, and he said: "By God, I pray for them the prayer of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace: I make the first two long and lighten the last two." (He would lengthen the first two units and lighten the last two units; and thus was the prayer of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace.) So Umar said: "That is what was thought of you."

And Sad said in his address: "By God, I am the first of the Arabs to shoot an arrow in the path of God; and we used to raid with the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, having no provision but the leaves of the acacia and this ḥublah plant, so that one of us would relieve himself as a sheep relieves itself, with nothing mixed in it. And now Banu Asad presume to discipline me over Islam! I should have failed indeed, and my striving would have gone astray."

And likewise the zealous young men of the Khawarij, when they shouted at Ali, may God be pleased with him, "You have disbelieved a hideous unbelief!" — he said: "Woe to you! How should I be the first to affirm the truth of him, and then disbelieve in him after his death?"

Those who go to excess in dealing with people and in appraising them do not look at anyone according to his precedence in Islam. These Companions whom they spoke against — the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, bore witness for them by name of the Garden, and God sent down in His Book His good pleasure with them and that what they did would not harm them. For whomever God is pleased with, with His greatest good pleasure after which there is no anger, his sins do not occur except forgiven. And even so these people appraise them, who do not reach so far as the strap of the sandal of one of those, nor even to the dust of his horse on a single day in the path of God.

For this reason Malik, may God have mercy on him, said to one of them when he heard him cursing some of the Emigrants and the Helpers — he called him and said to him: "Are you of the first Emigrants?" He said: "No." He said: "Then are you of the Helpers who gave shelter and support?" He said: "No." He said: "Then I bear witness by God that you are not of those who followed them in excellence — for God, exalted be He, said: {And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith} (Sūrat al-Ḥashr 59:10) — and you are cursing them."

Likewise, among this kind of excess is another excess, by going to extremes concerning persons and sanctifying them. For persons after the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, none of them is protected from error: they are practitioners of independent legal reasoning (ijtihād) who err and are right. We esteem the people of good, but we do not sanctify them. For that reason the community has agreed by consensus that the act of one who is not protected from error is not a binding proof.

These noble Companions, whose trials in Islam and their effect in it and their precedence in it we have spoken of, and what God and His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, bore witness for them — even so, what they did of errors, if anyone wishes to take them as a model in it, we do not accept that of him, because we know that it is an error; but it is an error forgiven in the case of the Companions, and we do not know whether it is forgiven in the case of one who follows their trace in it or not forgiven. So we prevent him from falling into it and stand between him and it.

This is what our esteem for them requires — not what the sanctification requires which some people adopt, even towards those below the Companions. For many people sanctify some of the living and some of the dead whom they lived alongside, so that he is never able to criticise in them what they opposed of the revealed law of God, and does not make them a place for scrutiny in any way whatever. Rather he holds that whoever opposes them, even in a matter in which he has strong evidence, deserves of punishment what Pharaoh's sorcerers deserved — to be crucified upon the trunks of palm trees. This kind of sanctification of persons is of the leading astray of people by Iblis.

Then among the kinds of obscurity relating to mixing with people is another kind of obscurity, which requires of a person that he attempt to take the whole of his own right, and attempt to fall short in the rights of people as much as he can. So he attempts to diminish people's things and to reduce their rights as much as he can, while his own right is to be full and complete, touched by no deficiency in any way whatever. This is the very perfection of the short-measuring of which God said: {Woe to those who give short measure — who, when they take by measure from people, take in full; and when they measure out to them or weigh out to them, give less. Do those not think that they will be raised up for a great day, a day when people will stand before the Lord of the worlds?} (Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn 83:1–6).

I recall that a man visited a relative of his and reminded him of a tie of kinship between them, wanting from him the right of that kinship; and he said: "Upon the head and the eye — but do you not recall that I have the like of this kinship also?" So when the right is his, he comes wanting his right; and when the right belongs to the other, he does not acknowledge it. This kind of obscurity is likewise widespread among people.

The cause of both kinds is the soiling of inner sight and its darkening because of what accumulates in it of acts of disobedience. For when acts of disobedience to God become numerous, inner sight is blackened, so that a person can hardly distinguish between truth and falsehood, and can hardly distinguish between right and error.

*When a man's conduct is evil, his suppositions become evil, and he holds true the imaginings he has grown used to; and he treats those who love him as enemies on the word of his enemy, and so comes to be in a night of darkened doubt.*

Then these two armies among the armies of Iblis — the obscurities and the appetites — nothing can stand in their way but patience and certainty. Patience is what stands before the appetite, so that a person does not fall into it and is patient in abstaining from the perishing appetite out of desire and longing for the abiding appetite: he desires the gardens of bliss; he desires the neighbourhood of God, mighty and majestic, in the highest Firdaws of the Garden beneath the Throne of the Merciful; he desires that his name be mentioned in the highest assembly, and that God draw near to him — for if he draws near a handspan, God draws near to him a cubit; and if he draws near a cubit, He draws near to him a fathom; and if he comes to Him walking, He comes to him at a run. Glory be to our Lord, how generous and how forbearing He is!

By that these obscurities cannot lead him astray, for between him and them is a fortified barrier; he cannot fall into them. And if Satan causes him to slip so that he falls into the edge of them, he remembers and hastens to repentance and seeking forgiveness: {Truly those who are God-conscious, when a visitation from Satan touches them, they remember, and behold, they see clearly. And their brothers — they draw them on into error, then they do not stop short} (Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:201–202).

The enmity of Iblis towards people is plain and clear, but its manifestations have not been studied by many people; many people are unaware of these manifestations.

I know some people who devote themselves utterly to perfecting their work and their jobs, and by that they suppose it to be an act of drawing near to God and a thing to be praised — while in reality it is an act of drawing near and a thing to be praised only in the sight of Iblis. You see the man whose job is in origin in a forbidden (ḥarām) occupation: he perfects it and lets nothing of the time escape him and does not fall short in that job which is forbidden and a defiance of God and His Messenger; and it is never recorded against him on any day that he was absent or late for the fixed working hours. And by this he supposes that he is doing well in work and that he is rendering a service — while the reality is that he is only drawing near to Iblis by what he does.

Iblis casts a false appearance over him: that he is bound by a contract and that he takes a salary for this work, so that perfecting it and setting it right is binding upon him. But the reality is that this contract is in its very origin null and void — for "whoever introduces into this affair of ours what is not of it, it is rejected." And with a contract by which God and His Messenger are defied, he would have done well to withdraw from it; and if he found no livelihood except to take of the salt of the earth and sell it, or of its firewood, or to sit in his house and be given charity by the Muslims, that would be better for him than such work, which is a defiance of God and His Messenger.

And you find others earning by the plainly forbidden and saying: "Some of the people of knowledge have mentioned, among the anomalous opinions, that earning by way of a doubtful matter is not objectionable." This is contrary to the reality: what you are earning by is not a doubtful matter — rather you know that it is forbidden, and if you reviewed yourself and sought a ruling of your own soul, you would not be content to meet God with it carried upon your neck.

And even so — even if it were a doubtful matter — who is it that commanded the doubtful matters after the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, forbade them and said: "The lawful is clear and the forbidden is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. So whoever guards against the doubtful matters has sought acquittal for his religion and his honour; and whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the forbidden, like a shepherd who grazes around a protected pasture and is on the verge of falling into it."

Has there come to you, after the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, a messenger from God?! What the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, brought is the truth in which there is no abrogation and no supplementing and no changing. God sent down upon him: {Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and approved Islam for you as religion} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:3). So what was not religion on that day is not religion today.

This accursed enemy casts a false appearance over people in various matters. In their conceptions and their creeds they set out from principles that are not of what the noble Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, brought, and they attach them to what he brought and suppose them to be part of its completion. So they suppose that abandoning those innovations or those superstitions is a deficiency in the religion — while in reality it is the soundness of the religion and its uprightness. Had they reviewed themselves they would have known that the religion cannot be added to after the death of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and that no revelation can come down after the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, passed to God.

Among the most astonishing of that is that I heard an imam of one of the recognised mosques speaking about one of the innovations, saying: "Yes, it was not known in the first generation; rather its being laid down in law was in the fourth century of the Hijrah." — Who is the messenger who was sent in the fourth century of the Hijrah? And this is an imam and a preacher who directs the Muslims, and he says: "It was not known in the first generation; rather its being laid down in law was in the fourth century of the Hijrah."

This kind is of the astonishing false appearance cast by Iblis. And I am certain that this imam intended nothing but good, and that had he reviewed himself a little before he spoke, he would have known that the wells cannot hold this. What came out of his narrow mouth the mouths of wells cannot hold — so how should the mouth of this imam hold it?

Likewise we find others bringing things of this sort, exceedingly strange, which the man of reason who is not educated at all and has no share of knowledge rejects; and if the small child who is upon the innate disposition hears them he says: "Glory be to You — this is a grave slander." And even so you find the elders who are taken as models believing them to be correct and to be the truth upon which there is no dust.

I recall that a small boy, still studying in the first year of preparatory school, was told by his uncle that the poles of the earth are seven: one of them is the one who holds the heavens, another is the one who holds the earths, another is the one who holds the seas, another is the one who holds the mountains, and so on to the end of that list. So the boy said to him: "Uncle, what have they left for our Lord, glorified and exalted? Did God, exalted be He, not say: {Truly God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease} (Sūrat Fāṭir 35:41), and He holds the sky from falling upon the earth except by His leave? How should those be holding this whole universe and no dominion remain for our Lord, glorified and exalted?"

There is no doubt that the levels of the two men in knowledge differ, and that the elder has a share of knowledge that cannot be compared with the younger's; but the younger is upon the innate disposition, and the elder has become entangled in a snare among the snares of Iblis, so that he flounders in it and does not know the way out.

The like of this is that many people, when they hear someone rejecting one of the innovations which they found some of their contemporaries upon — and there has never ceased to be one who rejects it in the religion of God, because no age can be devoid of one who upholds God's proof; no age among the ages in any land is devoid of one who upholds God's proof, rejecting what the revealed law has rejected — even so, he clings to it with a great clinging.

I met one of the brothers of the people of these lands, and there he was immersed in tobacco in the foulest way imaginable, and the sound of his chest and its wheezing was like the wheezing of a cauldron, from the severity of his illness and the effect upon his lungs. So I said to him: "My brother, do you not know that this is harmful to your health and that there is no good in it, and that what contains pure, evident harm has been forbidden?" He said: "My father, may God have mercy on him, was among the righteous and the scholars, and he used to smoke." So I said: "My brother, you did not follow him in knowledge and righteousness; rather you chose the basest thing he had and followed him in that. He was among the scholars and the righteous and you did not follow him in that. You do not claim knowledge and righteousness; you claim only smoking. And this is the basest thing your father had, may God have mercy on him — so you followed him in nothing but the meanest thing."

This kind, regrettably, is still widespread in many of our environments and in many of the countries of the Muslim world. You find a man shifting the discussion from a scholarly matter with clear evidence to a side matter that is not a place for discussion, or building upon it such implications as do not occur to the mind. So if a discussion takes place on a scholarly question relating to some of the rights of divinity and the difference between them and the rights of the servants, he shifts that into a war between you and the Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, for example; and when you affirm the rights of divinity for God, the One, the Subduer, alone, having no partner, his rage becomes intense, because he supposes that by that you are diminishing the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace.

This poor man does not know that this which you have brought is what the Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, brought, and it is that for the sake of which he was honoured. For the Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, was honoured by his message with which God sent him — and it is the message of the oneness of God, and it is the message of sincerity: {And they were commanded only to worship God, making the religion sincerely His, upright; and to establish the prayer and to give the zakat. And that is the upright religion} (Sūrat al-Bayyinah 98:5).

This poor man does not grasp that. Rather he holds that everyone who sets out one of the sunnah practices of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, in distinguishing between the right of God and the rights of the servants is an enemy of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace. And he holds that whoever rejects one who has innovated in the religion of God what God did not permit, and what His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, did not bring, thereby wishes to demolish one of the pillars of the Islamic creed, or wishes to cut off the supply that comes from the noble Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace. And this supply which he imagines for the innovation is not a supply from the Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace; rather it is an inspiration among the inspirations of Satan and a supply among the supplies of Satan. For the Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace — his supply is faith and knowledge and the revelation sent down: {Say: I only warn you by the revelation} (Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:45) — and his supply cannot be superstition and misleading innovation. This cannot be conceived in any way whatever.

This work which Satan has striven for and made manifest, and which the rabble of people have followed him in, a person may find some room for in ignorant circles; but its spread is to be thought strange in educated circles, whose small children read the Book of God and complete its memorisation at eight, and read what is accessible of the sunnah of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and of the rulings of the revealed law — and even so this superstition and this kind of astonishing charlatanry runs in their veins.

This kind of work of Iblis must inevitably meet resistance, and no age of the ages of this community has been devoid of resistance to it. In these lands in which we are — and they are the lands of knowledge and of scholars — no age of the ages has been devoid of a number of scholars who sacrificed their relationships and their interests among people, seeking to help God and His Messenger and to reject error and falsehood, and who stand against this falsehood with a strong standing; and they may suffer some harassments and problems, but they stand fast and are patient. The like of these are many in every age of the ages of this land and in every time of its times.

The men who used to stand up for God, glorified and exalted, with the truth in the face of Iblis, and who struggled against the spread of caprice among people, discharged the duty that was upon them in their own time. And this time is your time today: you are the responsible ones and you are their successors who have remained after them. So whatever occurs of shame and fault, you bear it, and it is not borne by the fathers and grandfathers who discharged the duty that was upon them.

And your time is not like their time. Their time, as we have mentioned, was one in which the seeking of knowledge was widespread and people preferred the seeking of knowledge to the seeking of this world. Today ignorance has spread and the carpet of knowledge has been rolled up and many of its study-centres have been closed, and people — except those upon whom God has had mercy — have come to waver back into utter ignorance.

So your responsibility, company of believers who affirm God's oneness, who are sincere and truthful, is that you help God and His Messenger, and that you return people to the white clear way, and that you lie in wait for Iblis — and that this be with gentleness and mildness and kindness, and be in the correct manner which the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, brought; and that you not address people with coarse speech, which has no effect except the contrary one; and that you lead them to Islam by the easiest paths and by the shortest roads; and that you thereby be successful in your calling and travellers upon the road of the prophets.

If you do that, you will have realised your enmity towards Iblis which God commanded you with, and you will have freed yourselves from the misleading caprices, and freed yourselves likewise from the portions of the selves which always summon you to attempt to gain victory by falsehood. And among the rights of people upon you is that you help them against Iblis, for they are in a confrontation with him.

This immense confrontation requires of the people of understanding in religion that they come forward with sound contemporary independent legal reasoning (ijtihād) which makes the paths easy for people in the matters that have arisen and were not previously known. For the Imam Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: "Judgements arise for people in proportion to what they have introduced of moral corruption." And that has been transmitted from a number of the imams of the early generations.

I know that a number of those who possess vast wealth whose origin is from the forbidden, and who dispose of it today, find it burdensome to rid themselves of this wealth — and that is because of the social and economic level at which they live and at which their children will live after them. So it is upon us not to help Satan against them. If we want to free them from the forbidden, let us attempt to come forward with a new independent legal reasoning that frees them from the forbidden and does not cast them into hardship, and does not cut off for them the road to guidance and uprightness.

I have exercised independent legal reasoning and have seen a procedure which requires that those who repent be addressed by saying to them: "Take account of yourselves and look at what you have of forbidden wealth, and take it by way of a loan, and hand over from it, every such-and-such period, such-and-such to the orphans, or to the charitable causes among the Muslims, or to the poor — even from among your relatives; and by that you free yourselves from the forbidden by instalments and by degrees."

I have put this legal opinion (fatwā) to those of the men of independent legal reasoning and of issuing legal opinions whom I have met, and they agreed to it. A number of those who repented and turned back have acted upon it — we reckon them so, and God is their reckoner — and they were able to free themselves from the forbidden by instalments, and for their profits and their businesses to remain the property of themselves and of their children after them.

People are in great need of this kind in our time. For those who do not exercise this kind of independent legal reasoning may cut off the road of repentance and uprightness for those who wish to repent — and even so, they still have weakness before enticements and before caprices.

We ask God, glorified and exalted, to grant us success in what He loves and is pleased with, and to make all our deeds sincerely for His noble face, and not to place in them any portion or share for anyone. And may God bless and grant peace to our Prophet Muhammad and to his family and his Companions all together.

flags.arabic: فإذا يئس من إدخاله في الشرك حاول إيقاعه في إحدى الموبقات … حاول أن يترك بعض السنن المكملة للفرائض … المكروهات التي تهوي به إلى المحرمات … بعض المندوبات التي هي سياج دون السنن والسنن سياج دون الفرائض … خلاف الأولى … شغله بالمندوب عن الواجب وبالمفضول عن الفاضل … الغلو في الفرائض … الغلو أيضا في بغض المحرمات … حتى يترك بعض ما هو حلال له فيحرم ما أحل الله
flags.context: The ladder of Satan's successive attempts, the structural centre of the lecture.
options: Map every grade to its fixed English rendering and keep the eleven rungs distinct, as done here
Simplify the ladder into a smaller number of stages
flags.note: THE MOST RULING-DENSE PASSAGE IN THIS SLICE, and the one where a slip would do most damage. The Sheikh walks down eleven rungs in strict order, and the whole force of the passage is that each rung is a distinct legal grade. Every one has been mapped to its fixed rendering under style guide 3: farāʾiḍ as obligatory duties, sunan as sunnah acts, mandūbāt as recommended acts, makrūhāt as disliked acts, muḥarramāt as forbidden acts, khilāf al-awlā as contrary to what is preferable, wājib as obligatory. Two points need a reviewer's eye. First, the Sheikh here treats mandūb and sunnah as DISTINCT and ordered grades — 'the recommended acts, which are a fence before the sunnah acts, and the sunnah acts are a fence before the obligatory duties' — which is the graded Maliki usage style guide 3 requires be preserved; the glossary renders both mandūb and mustaḥabb as 'recommended', so the English risks flattening a distinction he is explicitly building an argument on. Second, the last two rungs are rungs of EXCESS, not of laxity: going beyond the required limit in the obligatory duties, and hating the forbidden so far as to abandon what is lawful 'and so forbid what God has made lawful'. Those must not be read as endorsements of scrupulosity; the Sheikh counts them as Satan's work exactly as he counts the rungs of laxity.

flags.arabic: وقد اجتهدت فرأيت عملية تقتضي أن يخاطب أولئك التائبون … وخذوه على وجه القرض وسلموا منه كل فترة كذا وكذا لليتامى أو لجهات الخير في المسلمين أو للفقراء حتى من أقاربكم … وقد عرضت هذه الفتوى على رجال الاجتهاد والإفتاء من لقيت منهم فوافقوا عليها
flags.context: The closing section of the lecture.
options: Render as the Sheikh's own legal opinion, with its terms exactly as given and its unspecified quantities left unspecified, as done here
Supply a period and a proportion to make the procedure operable
Withhold the passage from display pending confirmation from the Sheikh's office
flags.note: THIS IS A LIVE FATWĀ OF THE SHEIKH'S OWN, not a reported position, and it has direct financial consequences for anyone who acts on it. Three things must survive exactly. First, the mechanism: the repentant holder is to treat the unlawful wealth as a LOAN ('ʿalā wajhi al-qarḍ') owed by him, and to discharge it in instalments to orphans, Muslim charitable causes or the poor, including his own relatives. Second, the quantities: the Sheikh says 'every such-and-such period, such-and-such', leaving BOTH the interval and the amount unspecified. Nothing has been supplied, and nothing must be: a rendering that named a period or a fraction would be inventing the operative content of a fatwā. Third, the claimed corroboration: he says he put it to those of the people of ijtihād and iftāʾ whom he had met and they agreed — he names none of them, and no names have been supplied. Anyone intending to act on this must go back to the Sheikh's office; the English must not be published in a form that reads as a self-contained procedure.

flags.arabic: لكن الواقع أن ذلك العقد في أصله لاغ … فإذا لم يجد معاشا إلا أن يأخذ من ملح الأرض فيبيعه أو من حطبها، أو أن يجلس في بيته فيتصدق عليه المسلمون لكان ذلك خيرا له
flags.context: On a person employed in a forbidden occupation.
options: that contract is in its very origin null and void
that contract is in its origin void (bāṭil)
that contract is in its origin defective (fāsid)
flags.note: A validity ruling, and the word the Sheikh uses is 'lāghin' (null), not bāṭil and not fāsid. It has therefore NOT been mapped onto either glossary term, since the Maliki distinction between bāṭil and fāsid carries consequences he does not here engage. Note that the ruling concerns the contract's validity, not merely the sinfulness of the work: he holds that perfecting such work is an act of drawing near to Iblis, that the employee should withdraw from the contract, and that selling salt or firewood or living on charity would be better. He does not define which occupations fall under this, and no definition has been supplied.

flags.arabic: وقد ذكر أهل العلم من المتأخرين أن السياسة لدى المتأخرين وبالأخص في العالم العربي هي مثل الخمر والميسر … ولذلك تشهدون في بلادنا أن أرحاما كثيرة قطعت بسبب خلافات سياسية وانتماءات لأحزاب
flags.context: On Satan's means of sowing enmity.
options: Translate exactly as given, as done here
Render the comparison less sharply
flags.note: The Sheikh reports, attributing it to 'some of the later people of knowledge' and not to himself, that party politics in the Arab world functions as wine and gambling do in the verse — as a means by which Satan sows enmity. He names no scholar. He then applies it to his own country in his own voice, describing families divided by party affiliation. The attribution boundary between the reported opinion and his own application has been kept visible (style guide 1). Note that this is an analogy about the effect of partisanship, NOT a ruling that political participation is forbidden, and the English must not be read as one.

flags.arabic: أذكر أن ولدا صغيرا … حدثه عمه أن أقطاب الأرض سبعة أحدهم هو الممسك بالسماوات … وهذا المدد الذي يتوهمه هو للبدعة ليس مددا من الرسول (ص) وإنما هو وحي من وحي الشيطان
flags.context: Two passages in the later part of the lecture.
options: Translate exactly as given, as done here
Render the polemic in more neutral terms
flags.note: These two passages are a sustained polemic against doctrines and practices associated with the Sufi orders — the cosmology of the 'poles' (aqṭāb) who sustain the created order, and the notion of spiritual supply (madad) reaching the living from the Prophet. The Sheikh calls the second 'an inspiration among the inspirations of Satan'. The Sufi orders are the dominant religious form in Mauritania and across much of West Africa, and he names no order and no person. Translated faithfully, neither softened nor strengthened, as style guide 6 requires; a reviewer should weigh the communal charge before publication.

flags.arabic: ألا تعلم أن هذا مضر بصحتك وأنه لا خير فيه وقد نهيت عما فيه الضرر المحض البين؟
flags.context: The Sheikh's exchange with a smoker.
options: Render the rebuke without assigning a ruling to smoking, as done here
Render it as a ruling that smoking is forbidden (ḥarām)
Render it as a ruling that smoking is disliked (makrūh)
flags.note: The Sheikh rebukes smoking as harmful and as containing no good, and invokes the general prohibition of what carries pure and evident harm — but he does NOT name a ruling for smoking in this passage, and the passive 'nuhīta' ('you have been forbidden') leaves the grade unstated. Style guide 6 forbids resolving a question he left open, so the English states no grade. A reader should not be able to take either ḥarām or makrūh out of this record.

flags.arabic: ولذلك أجمعت الأمة على أن فعل غير المعصوم ليس بحجة … لكنه خطأ مغفور في حق الصحابة، ولا ندري هل يغفر في حق من يقتفي أثرهم فيه أو لا يغفر
flags.context: On esteeming the Companions without sanctifying them.
options: Preserve the full reasoning chain including the agnostic clause, as done here
Render only the conclusion that the Companions' errors are not to be imitated
flags.note: A careful usūlī passage that must not be compressed. The Sheikh states a claim of consensus (ijmāʿ) that the act of one not protected from error is not a binding proof; then applies it to the Companions; then deliberately leaves open whether an imitator's repetition of a Companion's error would be forgiven ('we do not know whether it is forgiven … or not forgiven'). That open clause is the hinge of the argument and style guide 6 forbids closing it. He gives no source for the consensus claim and none has been supplied.

flags.arabic: «إذا ساء فعل المرء ساءت ظنونه** وصدق ما يعتاده من توهم** وعادى محبيه بقول عدوه** فأصبح في ليل من الشك مظلم»
flags.context: On the darkening of inner sight by sin.
options: Render as two lines of verse in prose, as done here
Reproduce the source's asterisk hemistich separators
flags.note: Two lines of verse, with the hemistichs separated in the source by double asterisks — a transcription convention not used elsewhere in this slice. Style guide 4: rendered as prose in italics with the Arabic retained in the bilingual pane; no rhymed English has been attempted. The poet is not named. The final word is printed 'muẓlim' where the rhyme requires 'muẓlimi'.

flags.arabic: فقد قامت فرقة القدرية ثم فرقة الجبرية وقبل ذلك فرقة الخوارج وبعدهم فرقة الشيعة وهكذا
flags.context: On sects arising when the armies stop campaigning.
options: Report the sequence exactly as the Sheikh gives it, as done here
Reorder the sects chronologically
flags.note: The Sheikh's sequence is itself chronologically loose — he places the Khawarij 'before that' and the Shia 'after them', which cuts across the order in which he names the Qadariyyah and Jabriyyah. Style guide 6 forbids silently fixing it, so the order stands as he gives it. Naming the Shia among the sects that arose from idleness carries a sectarian charge that a reviewer should note.

flags.arabic: أثر موقوف رواه الترمذي الحكيم بلا إسناد في نوادر الأصول
flags.context: The anecdote of the man who answered a Qur'anic and prophetic proof with a weak report.
options: Leave the name in the source's order and identify the work, as done here
Correct to 'al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī'
flags.note: The scholar is al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, author of the Nawādir al-Uṣūl; the source inverts the two parts of the name. Not silently corrected, per style guide 11. The grading terms in the anecdote have been mapped exactly: 'athar mawqūf' as a report stopping at a Companion, and 'bi-lā isnād' as without a chain of transmission.

flags.arabic: التي يقرأ أولادها الصغار كتاب الله ويكملوا حفظه في الثامنة
flags.context: On educated circles in which superstition nonetheless spreads.
options: complete its memorisation at eight
complete its memorisation in the eighth year
flags.note: 'Fī al-thāminah' most naturally means at the age of eight, which is the reading the English follows and which fits the Mauritanian maḥḍarah tradition the Sheikh is describing. The verb 'yukmilū' is printed without its final nūn, a slip in the transcript. Flagged rather than corrected.

This is a complete lecture transcript (dars), not a sermon: it opens with the basmalah, the greeting of peace and 'ammā baʿd', and closes with a supplication and the prayer upon the Prophet, with no two-part structure and no sermon formulae. It is typed as a transcript accordingly.
This record uses '(ṣ)' throughout as an abbreviation for the prayer upon the Prophet, as ID 491 does. The English expands it; body_ar preserves the abbreviation.

The lecture is built as a taxonomy and should be displayed so the structure is visible: Satan's eleven successive attempts, then his two armies (appetites and obscurities), each divided and subdivided — appetites into sensory and non-material; obscurities into those in dealing with God (creedal and devotional, the devotional in turn walled by excess and by negligence) and those in dealing with people (appraisal of others, and short-measuring of their rights). The divisions are the argument, and they have been preserved rather than smoothed into continuous prose.

CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY, on two counts. First, the eleven-rung ladder touches every one of the five rulings in sequence and is the passage in this slice where a mistranslation would most directly misattribute a ruling; the Maliki grading of mandūb below sunnah below farḍ is load-bearing there and is flagged. Second, the closing section is a live fatwā of the Sheikh's own on discharging unlawful wealth by instalments, with real financial consequences, whose operative quantities he deliberately leaves unspecified. It must not be displayed as a self-contained procedure.

EDITORIAL REVIEW REQUIRED. The lecture contains sustained polemic against doctrines associated with the Sufi orders, which are the dominant religious form in the Sheikh's own country; a passage comparing party politics to wine and gambling; a ruling that employment contracts in forbidden occupations are null; and the naming of the Shia among sects that arose from idleness. All are translated faithfully and none is softened. Style guide 12: publication decisions belong to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

Note the lecture's own restraint, which should not be lost in excerpting: the Sheikh twice counts EXCESS as Satan's work alongside laxity; he warns against the student of knowledge turning himself into a judge who issues verdicts without qualification; he insists the Companions are esteemed and not sanctified; and he closes by instructing his audience to address people with gentleness and not with coarse speech. Any excerpt of the polemical passages that drops these would misrepresent the text.
